knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms

question.:question/worked-solution:
We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{13x-1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{13x}{x}-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (13-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =13\int \,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =13x-\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{13x-1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =13x-\ln|x|+C \\  & =13x-\ln|x|-\ln K \\  & =13x-(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =13x-\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{26}{3}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{26}{3x}\text{d}x & =\frac{26}{3}\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{26}{3}\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=\frac{26}{3}\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $\frac{26}{3}\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{26}{3x}\text{d}x & =\frac{26}{3}\ln|x|+C \\  & =\frac{26}{3}\ln|x|+\frac{26}{3}\ln K \\  & =\frac{26}{3}(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =\frac{26}{3}\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{13}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{13}{x}+\frac{169}{4{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+13\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\frac{169}{4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+13\ln|x|+\frac{169{x}^{-2+1}}{4(-2+1)}+C \\  & =x+13\ln|x|-\frac{169}{4x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=13\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $13\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{13}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{169}{4x}+13\ln|x|+13\ln K \\  & =x-\frac{169}{4x}+13(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =x-\frac{169}{4x}+13\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
